verses.1: Al-Mizan explains sharḥ al-ṣadr as a breast opened by divine light, tranquility, and comfort. In the sequence of the first three verses, it means that the Prophet was capacitated to receive revelation and bear the hardships and harassment of conveying it; his sacred soul was fully prepared for what God placed within it.
verses.2: Al-Mizan defines wizr as a heavy load and inqāḍ al-ẓahr as a conspicuous burden that breaks the back; its removal is the removal of the felt burden. Contextually, God made the causes of the Prophet’s success in his mission cohere, relieving the weight of the message, the call, and its consequences after expanding his breast. It notes that some exegetes linked this to a report of angels opening his chest, but judges proposed meanings involving pre-mission misconduct, ignorance, bereavement, infallibility, or the community’s sins to be weak or absurd in context.

verses.4: Al-Mizan reads the juxtaposition of ‘raise’ after ‘lower’ as the elevation of the Prophet’s reputation above other people. It identifies its clearest instance in the two testimonies of faith, where his name accompanies God’s, and in the five daily prayers, where Muslims mention both.
verses.5: Al-Mizan takes the verse as the reason for lifting the Prophet’s burden and raising his name: the mission, rejection, disparagement, and attempts to erase his name were eased when people accepted the call and his name was elevated. This exemplifies God’s continuing custom of ease after hardship, perhaps also the impermanence of events. Al-ʿusr denotes hardship as a genus (jins), not every hardship exhaustively (istighrāq). It rejects al-Zamakhsharī’s reading of consolation over believers’ poverty and a later ease of war spoils: the Prophet knew the opposition sprang from disdain and defiance, enrichment did not win the people over, and most had already been declared unbelieving (36:7-10) and (2:6). If the sūrah is Meccan, triumph and Islam’s elevation after abasement is more plausible.
verses.6: Al-Mizan treats the repetition as emphasis and affirmation. It reports an interpretation that makes the verse independent and infers two eases for one hardship because repeated definite al-ʿusr normally denotes the same hardship while repeated indefinite yusran need not denote the same ease, but adds that this linguistic rule is not universal.
verses.7: Al-Mizan addresses the Prophet and draws the command from the preceding favors and the principle of ease after hardship. Once obligations leave him free, he is to exert himself in worship and prayer and ardently seek God, through whom rest is embedded in exhaustion and ease in hardship. Recommended acts after obligatory ones and duʿāʾ after ṣalāh are specific applications; readings about returning from battle or turning from worldly matters to the hereafter are implausible.
